decision_lens: Derivations over an append-only log are only correct if the invalidation strategy is complete. Incomplete invalidation produces stale derived state that looks valid. In a century-scale simulation, an unbounded event log with derivations computed on read is a latency time-bomb — not on day one, but after the first 500-year campaign. The question is not whether the derivation model is elegant (it is) but whether its performance assumptions survive the load described in the North Star.
focus: Whether the derivation model and event-log claims in the brainstorm hold up under long-running simulation, cost-hint invalidation strategy for century-scale event logs, replay and snapshot concerns for Mind-scale time
name: fd-eventsourced-sim-derivation-model
persona: Apply the perspective of an event-sourced systems practitioner who has designed and debugged CQRS/ES simulations where time is a first-class concern, encountered unbounded event-log growth in production, and diagnosed derivation cache invalidation bugs that only appear after hundreds of thousands of events.
review_areas: The North Star describes Minds with 600-year histories whose behaviour is 'a derivation over that history.' If derivations are computed on read from the full event log (the Phase 1 model), a 600-year-old GSV Mind with continuous facet evolution events will have an event log of potentially millions of entries. The brainstorm mentions this concern in timescale model option (i) — 'designing derivation cost hints and invalidation strategy that don't blow up on long event logs' — but treats it as a Phase 1 derivation model compatibility claim without specifying the invalidation strategy that makes it tractable. The claim needs a design sketch, not a deferral.

The LlmCurated cost hint for ship names has an invalidation trigger: 're-roll when a significant scar lands.' But the brainstorm does not define 'significant scar' in terms the derivation system can evaluate. Scar significance presumably depends on the scar's facet-delta magnitude relative to the Mind's current facet state — which is itself a derivation. This creates a potential dependency cycle: the name-derivation depends on scar-significance, which depends on the current-facet derivation, which depends on the event log. If the scar-significance computation is also a derivation, the invalidation chain is recursive and the system needs a topologically sorted invalidation order, which the brainstorm does not mention.

The brainstorm recommends timescale model (i) for the migration MVP ('single tick, derivations carry the load') and (iii) for the Culture game endpoint ('hierarchical composition'). These two models have fundamentally different event-log structures: in (i), all events share a single logical tick sequence; in (iii), individual Soul events and civ-Soul aggregate events live in different time domains. Migrating from (i) to (iii) mid-project requires either retaining the full event log in (i) format or defining a snapshot/migration strategy. The brainstorm explicitly defers this but does not flag that the choice of (i) now creates a migration cost to (iii) later — the event-log format is effectively the schema and schemas are hard to migrate.

Aggregation Souls (expansion item 4) require that a civ-Soul's facets are projections of its member Souls' facets. In an event-sourced model, this means either: (a) the aggregation is a derivation computed on read from all member Soul event logs (scales poorly with civ size and history length), or (b) the aggregation is itself event-sourced (the civ-Soul receives synthetic events when member facets cross thresholds). Option (b) requires a new event type ('aggregate-threshold-crossed') and a trigger mechanism — neither of which is in the Phase 1 design. The brainstorm treats aggregation Souls as a future concern but does not acknowledge that their design is constrained by the event model chosen now.

The FacetEvolutionPolicy (expansion item 2) is described as making the ±20 cap a declarative catalogue property. In an event-sourced model, applying a new policy to historical events is a replay concern: does a policy change apply retroactively (replaying history under new caps) or only to future events? The brainstorm does not specify, but the answer has significant implications for simulation consistency — a Mind that was at +23 Curiosity under an old policy would be clamped to +20 retroactively under a new one, changing its archetype derivation.

The brainstorm proposes that the Culture itself is a Soul with scars from historical Contact catastrophes — scars that 'no living Mind witnessed firsthand.' In an event-sourced model, a scar is a FacetAppend event on a Soul's log. A civilisation-scale scar must be an event on the civ-Soul's log, not on any individual Mind's log. This means the civ-Soul's event log must be authoritative for civilisation-level historical events, separate from individual Mind logs. The doc does not address how civilisation-scale events are written, who writes them (the game engine? a special SC agent?), or how they are ordered relative to individual Mind events across the timescale boundary.

severity_examples.condition: If the migration MVP uses timescale model (i) and derivations are computed by scanning the full event log, then a 100-turn playthrough with hourly facet updates per Mind produces O(minds * turns * events-per-turn) events before any compaction. At grand-strategy scale (hundreds of Minds), this is O(10^7) events per simulated year. The brainstorm claims this fits the Phase 1 derivation model but provides no cost-hint or compaction design that demonstrates tractability.
severity_examples.scenario: Unbounded event-log growth with on-read derivation at century scale

severity_examples.condition: If scar significance is a derivation and ship-name is a derivation that depends on scar significance, and both share the same event log, the invalidation system must detect and handle this dependency. Without topological sort of derivations, marking scar-significance-changed as a ship-name invalidation trigger produces either double-computation or stale names after every scar event.
severity_examples.scenario: Derivation invalidation cycle between scar-significance and ship-name derivation

severity_examples.condition: Choosing timescale model (i) for the MVP produces a single-sequence event log. Migrating to model (iii) later requires either a snapshot-and-restart or an event-log migration that reattributes events to per-scale sub-logs. This cost is not acknowledged in the brainstorm's deferral of the timescale question.
severity_examples.scenario: Event-log schema lock-in from timescale model (i) choice

success_hints: Check each claim that uses the word 'derivation' and ask whether the derivation's invalidation trigger is specified — unspecified triggers are latent stale-state bugs
Look for any derivation that depends on another derivation and flag the dependency as requiring explicit ordering in the invalidation system
Verify that each deferred timescale design option is characterised by its event-log format — deferring the model choice is only safe if all options produce compatible log formats

Check whether the aggregation Soul design requires new event types or event producers not present in Phase 1 and flag these as migration-critical blockers if expansion item 4 is needed before the Culture game
task_context: The document proposes an event-sourced personality engine (Palettice) as the substrate for a century-scale grand-strategy game and as the migration target for a working personality system (shadow-work). This review focuses on whether the derivation and event-log design claims are sound at the scale the North Star describes, and whether deferred design decisions create load-bearing technical debt in the event model.
